g.text: Name:
Date:
OCT
Edison tests a long-lasting lamp
What clue would you check first on October 21?
Have you ever wondered why a small calendar box can open a much bigger
story? On October 21, Thomas Edison demonstrated a practical
incandescent lamp that stayed lit for many hours in October 1879. The
research record places this event in 1879, so the class can compare that
year with a nearby starting year of 1871. The title card says “Edison
tests a long-lasting lamp,” and it invites readers to look for the
problem, invention, creature, or challenge behind the headline. A
history detective does not need to memorize every detail; the detective
notices which clues can be checked and which numbers can be used
carefully. In this classroom version, the event-year clue ends in 9; for
the worksheet, each museum panel gets 11 labels, and the display repeats
that set across 2 panels. The passage also names 2 clues that can be set
aside after the first round. The timeline comparison uses 1871 and a gap
of 8 years, while the October label 21 helps us connect the math back to
the story. The source is National Park Service, so the event claim is
not invented for the worksheet. After reading, ask what you would check
first, whether the display tells the same story, and how a number can
describe a real event without becoming the whole event. History becomes
easier to remember when a reader asks a question, checks a source, and
then explains the clue in their own words.
